instruction: Someone keeps trying bad passwords on my box. Which log records failed logins and how do I read it?
response: Failed login attempts are collected in /var/log/btmp. The file is not plain text, so you view it with the lastb command rather than opening it in an editor, while successful logins and logouts are tracked separately in wtmp.

instruction: Why do most files under /proc show a size of zero even though cat prints real data?
response: Nothing is actually stored on disk there; the entries are a window into the running kernel, and the content is generated at the moment you read it. That is why a process directory like /proc/460 or a file like interrupts looks empty in a listing but still returns live information.

instruction: Can I safely wipe everything under /var/cache like I'd clear /var/spool?
response: Cache data is locally generated and can be rebuilt, so removing it loses nothing important. Spool directories are different because they hold queued work such as mail, print jobs and cron tables that is waiting to be processed, so clearing them can throw away pending jobs.

instruction: How is single-quoting different from double-quoting a variable in Bash?
response: Double quotes block word splitting and most special characters, but $, backquotes and backslash keep their meaning, so "$var" is replaced by its value. Single quotes are the stricter form and treat everything literally, which means $var is not expanded at all.

instruction: I need to check a script's syntax without running it and also see what it does line by line. Which options help?
response: Use sh -n to check syntax without executing anything, sh -v to echo each line before it runs, and sh -x to show each command's expanded result in a shortened form. The -n and -v flags can be combined as -nv, and adding set -u makes the script abort on any unset variable.

instruction: My script with a for loop dies with 'syntax error: unexpected end of file'. Where do I start looking?
response: Check that every opening keyword has its closing partner, because a for loop missing its done is a classic cause. Bash only realises something is wrong when it reaches the end of the file, so the real mistake usually sits earlier than the line it reports.

instruction: Disk names like /dev/sdb change every time I plug drives in different orders. How do I mount a partition reliably?
response: Look up the partition's UUID with blkid or "lsblk -f", then refer to that instead of the device name. You can pass it to mount with the -U option, or put the UUID in /etc/fstab, and boot loaders can use it too.

instruction: How do strictatime, relatime and noatime behave differently on a mounted filesystem?
response: With strictatime every read updates the access time, which costs a disk write each time. Relatime, the default since Linux 2.6.30, only updates it on the first read or after a day, and noatime never updates it on reads. The last two exist to speed up normal read-heavy use.

instruction: Hard link or symlink: how do they differ when I run ln?
response: A hard link, made with "ln foo bar", is just another name for the same existing file. A symbolic link, made with "ln -s foo bar", is a special file that points at another file by name instead.

instruction: After the kernel loads, what does init do first and where does it look for instructions?
response: The kernel finds init in /sbin and starts it, and from then on init is the ancestor of every process that starts automatically. It begins by reading /etc/inittab, which sets up the environment, names the default run level and describes what each run level should start.

instruction: Why does Linux printing have two commands for most tasks, like lpq and lpstat, and does it matter which I use?
response: The pairs exist because old UNIX printing came in a BSD style and a SystemV style, and CUPS on Linux supports both. They are not perfectly identical, since lpq takes different options than lpstat and lprm is only almost the same as cancel, so just pick the set you are comfortable with.

instruction: A CD refuses to come out and the system keeps answering 'device busy'. What should I check?
response: Make sure no shell is still sitting inside the mount point, for example by running cd with no arguments, and that no graphical program is using the disc. Then run umount /mnt/cdrom or eject cdrom, and if it is still busy use lsof to find the process holding it rather than forcing the drive open.

instruction: How does getting IP masquerading into a kernel differ between the 2.2 and 2.4 series?
response: On 2.2 you select the masquerading options when configuring the kernel, and since some parts are modules you also have to run make modules. The 2.4 kernels dropped that compile-time option, so you enable network packet filtering instead, which replaces ipchains.

instruction: My laptop moves between two NIS domains. How should I write yp.conf so I don't have to edit it every time?
response: Add one `domain` line per NIS domain, like `domain winery server vbardolino` and `domain brewery server vstout`, and pick the right one at boot by setting the domain name with domainname. If you don't know the server for a domain, use the `broadcast` keyword and ypbind will take whichever server answers.

instruction: How can I stop a modem dial script from leaking my login details to other users running ps?
response: Don't put the chat script on the command line, since anyone can read a process's arguments with ps. Save it in a file, with the expected string on the left and the reply on the right, and start chat with `-f` plus the filename, for instance `chat -f dial-c3po` inside pppd's connect option.

instruction: Explain how a text-console login works.
response: init starts one getty per terminal, and getty reads the username and launches login, which asks for the password and then starts the shell if it checks out. When the shell exits or the login fails, init notices and spawns a fresh getty, since the kernel itself knows nothing about logins.

instruction: What do runlevels 0, 1 and 6 usually mean?
response: Runlevel 0 halts the system, runlevel 1 is single-user mode where only root works at the console, and runlevel 6 reboots the machine. Normal day-to-day multiuser operation is usually runlevel 3, and 5 is typically the same thing with a GUI started as well.

instruction: Does running a script with source behave differently from executing it directly?
response: Yes. With source, which is the same as the dot command, the commands run inside your current shell and the file doesn't need execute permission, so any variables it sets are still there afterwards. Running the script normally starts it in a subshell instead.

instruction: I want a daily cron job that emails root when any disk is at least 80% full. How would the script work?
response: Pull the usage percentages out of df -h with awk, sort them numerically, take the largest with tail -1 and strip the % sign with cut. An if test using -ge against an alert value of 80 then decides whether to pipe a warning into mail -s addressed to root, and cron runs the script daily.
